title: Ensure no LXD instance runs as a privileged container
description: security.privileged=true disables the user-namespace UID mapping, so root inside the container is root on the host. The audit loops over instances from "lxc list --format csv -c n" (default project) and inspects the expanded configuration (including profiles) of each; any truthy security.privileged fails the rule.
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Unprivileged containers (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command:
lxc info >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
names=$(lxc list --format csv -c n 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
bad=0
for n in $names; do
  cfg=$(lxc config show --expanded "$n" 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
  if printf '%s\n' "$cfg" | grep -Eiq '^[[:space:]]*security\.privileged:[[:space:]]*"?(true|1|yes|on)"?[[:space:]]*$'; then echo "privileged: $n"; bad=1; fi
done
[ "$bad" -eq 0 ] && echo compliant

remediation.command: For each reported instance (and any profile setting it): lxc config unset <instance> security.privileged (or lxc profile unset <profile> security.privileged), then restart the instance in a maintenance window; fix file ownership inside the rootfs if the instance was created privileged.

title: Ensure membership of the lxd group is limited to administrators
description: Members of the lxd group can talk to the LXD unix socket and therefore create privileged containers that mount the host filesystem; membership is equivalent to root. Group membership is site policy, so this is a review item.
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Restrict access to the LXD socket (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command: Run "getent group lxd" and confirm every listed user is an authorised host administrator. Also review "lxc config trust list" for unexpected client certificates and enable restricted certificates or projects for non-admin users.

remediation.command:
gpasswd -d lxd for unauthorised members; remove unexpected certificates with lxc config trust remove ; give limited users a restricted project (lxc config trust add --restricted --projects

).

title: Ensure the LXD remote API is not listening on all interfaces
description: core.https_address exposes the LXD REST API (full control of every instance and the host) over the network. The audit reads it with "lxc config get core.https_address" and passes when it is unset (local unix socket only) or bound to a specific address; it fails on wildcard binds such as [::], 0.0.0.0 or a bare :8443. The lxc client must reach the daemon (run as root or a member of the lxd group).
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Restrict remote API exposure (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command:
lxc info >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
v=$(lxc config get core.https_address 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
case "$v" in
  "[::]"*|0.0.0.0*|:*) echo "remote API listens on all interfaces: $v"; exit 1 ;;
esac
echo compliant

remediation.guidance: If remote access is not needed: lxc config unset core.https_address. Otherwise bind to the management interface only, e.g. lxc config set core.https_address 10.0.0.5:8443, and restrict port 8443 with the host firewall.

title: Ensure core.trust_password is not set
description: A trust password lets any client that knows it add its certificate as a fully trusted remote, and it is brute-forceable over the network. Use short-lived trust tokens (lxc config trust add) instead. The audit runs "lxc config get core.trust_password" (prints "true"/hash when set); newer LXD releases removed the key, which is reported as compliant.
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Remote client authentication (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command:
lxc info >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
v=$(lxc config get core.trust_password 2>/dev/null)
[ -z "$v" ] && echo compliant

title: Ensure LXD instances do not enable container nesting
description: security.nesting=true exposes /proc and /sys more widely and relaxes AppArmor so containers can run their own container runtimes, enlarging the escape surface. The audit loops over instances from "lxc list --format csv -c n" (default project) and fails if any expanded configuration sets security.nesting to a truthy value. Hosts that deliberately run Docker-in-LXD should document the exception.
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Container nesting (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command:
lxc info >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
names=$(lxc list --format csv -c n 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
bad=0
for n in $names; do
  cfg=$(lxc config show --expanded "$n" 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
  if printf '%s\n' "$cfg" | grep -Eiq '^[[:space:]]*security\.nesting:[[:space:]]*"?(true|1|yes|on)"?[[:space:]]*$'; then echo "nesting: $n"; bad=1; fi
done
[ "$bad" -eq 0 ] && echo compliant

remediation.command: lxc config unset <instance> security.nesting (or remove it from the profile), then restart the instance. Move workloads that need nested containers to a VM instance (lxc launch --vm).

title: Ensure LXD instances do not use raw.lxc or raw.apparmor overrides
description: raw.lxc and raw.apparmor inject low-level LXC/AppArmor directives that bypass LXD security defaults (for example lxc.apparmor.profile=unconfined or extra mounts). The audit loops over instances from "lxc list --format csv -c n" (default project) and fails if any expanded configuration contains these keys.
reference: CIS-style LXD hardening guidance - Raw configuration overrides (no CIS benchmark section; verify against your hardening standard)

audit.command:
lxc info >/dev/null 2>&1 || exit 1
names=$(lxc list --format csv -c n 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
bad=0
for n in $names; do
  cfg=$(lxc config show --expanded "$n" 2>/dev/null) || exit 1
  if printf '%s\n' "$cfg" | grep -Eq '^[[:space:]]*raw\.(lxc|apparmor):'; then echo "raw override: $n"; bad=1; fi
done
[ "$bad" -eq 0 ] && echo compliant

remediation.command: Review the directives, then lxc config unset <instance> raw.lxc / raw.apparmor (or remove them from the profile) and express any genuine need with supported keys (devices, security.syscalls.*). Restart the instance.
